files.review_note: Keep the opening, RFC clauses, signal-code comparison and mixed-classroom argument. Remove narrator commentary and assumptions about the reader; retain the practical scope limits.

edits.before:

Some of you run that exchange without a thought and couldn't state one rule

edits.before:
So the rules are not unknowable. Researchers have been writing them down for
over fifty years. They were written for other researchers, in a register
nobody outside the field reads, and then everyone went on behaving as if the
rules were self-evident. This is the engineering scandal the course is named
for. The protocol has documentation. It was never shipped to the users.
edits.after:
Researchers have been writing these rules down for over fifty years, for
other researchers. The protocol has documentation. It was never shipped to
the users.
edits.reason: Keep the deadpan punchline; remove the explanation of why it is an engineering scandal and the sweeping claim about readership.

edits.before:

what would count as an instance, you cannot check any claim you make about
it.** That is the difference between a specification and an opinion.
edits.after:
We read his abstract, not the paper, so this page does not list the six.
**Before testing a claim about greetings, say what would count as a greeting.**
edits.reason: Keep the evidence limit and usable method; remove the announcement of its significance and the closing maxim.

edits.before:

answer. The majority's version is a local implementation, and it is the one
this building runs.
edits.after:
The next section specifies **one local convention**: the handshake between
acquaintances passing in a corridor. Elsewhere, the same place in an exchange
can be used to ask a question and get an answer.
edits.reason: State the scope once, without turning a local working example into a universal claim about the building.

edits.before:

edits.before:

edits.before:

edits.reason: Retain the recorded result but remove the unsupported claims that negative events are its only condition and that all journal entries concern failed exchanges.

files.review_note: Keep the five audiences, practical scripts, study results and protected register break. Remove self-praise, let the scripts carry the teaching, and avoid promising that partial disclosure always succeeds or costs little.

edits.before:

edits.after:
A favourable first impression does not settle whether disclosure will help
someone at work. These studies ask different people, in different settings,
about different consequences.
edits.reason: Keep the distinction between study designs without putting recommendations into the participants’ mouths.

edits.before:

is not a decision aid --- it is a thumb on one side of the scale.
edits.after: Before deciding, put **not telling** in the ledger too.
edits.reason: State the practical next step once; the following study supplies the reason for it.

edits.before:

It is **not** the effort of concealing, and it is not whether you have told
anyone. It is **what you expect would happen if people knew**.
edits.after:
The predictor **anticipated stigma** is what you expect would happen if people
knew. It is not the effort of concealing, or whether you have told anyone.
edits.reason: Name the specific predictor directly instead of announcing an obvious reader mistake.

edits.before:

First, two people keeping the same thing to themselves, at the same cost in

edits.after:
Two people keeping the same thing to themselves, at the same cost in effort,
are not carrying the same weight. What separates them is a belief about the

edits.before:

edits.after:
That belief is something an **environment produces**. Which means a department
where disclosure is ordinary and adjustments are unremarkable is lowering a

edits.before: One more structural point, and it isn't this course's invention.

edits.before:
We read the abstract and not the paper, so we are not going to reproduce their

What the citation earns is the shape: **disclosure has levels rather than an on

interchangeable. The machinery, it turns out, is largely shared.
edits.after:
We read the abstract, not the paper, so we will not reproduce their levels.
The five audiences and partial-disclosure scripts below are the course's own.
The paper gives us the idea of **levels rather than an on switch**; its

edits.after: **You can disclose a need without the label.**

files.review_note: Retain the coefficients and explicit correlation caveat; remove a second, categorical explanation of why this is the whole argument.

edits.before: That "independent of diagnosis" is the whole argument. The judgement isn't attached to a category of person. It attaches to a property of a reading — and a reading has two parties in it, one of whom is doing the reading. Which is the double empathy problem with a correlation coefficient on it.
edits.reason: The preceding paragraph already connects readability to judgement. Remove the second, more categorical interpretation and keep the authors' correlation caveat.

files.review_note: Retain: a compact account of the experiment with a useful warning against treating its speed as everyday advice.
Retain the reported themes and quotation; separate masking duration from recovery time and remove the course-vindication narrative.

edits.before: 277 autistic adults on what camouflaging costs and what it buys --- and the finding that what damages people most is the amount of time they spend doing it.
edits.after: 277 autistic adults on the costs and benefits of camouflaging, and the time they spend doing it.
edits.reason: The original summary turns a qualified conclusion into a definitive ranking of damage.

edits.before: Two sentences from the abstract do most of the work for week 6. “Time spent camouflaging is what seems to be most damaging” — the course's ledger had already priced masking in *recovery hours*, so it guessed the right axis and can now cite it rather than assert it. And the reason given for needing so much time is society's lack of awareness and acceptance, which is the ledger's pressure column with a source behind it. The paper's own lay summary says reducing the pressure to camouflage would benefit everyone in society, which is the course's mixed-room claim in the authors' words rather than the course's.
edits.after: The abstract concludes: “Time spent camouflaging is what seems to be most damaging”. Week 6 uses these accounts to discuss cost and pressure. Its *recovery hours* remain a planning device; time spent camouflaging does not establish a measure of time needed to recover. Participants identified society's lack of awareness and acceptance as a reason they needed to camouflage. The authors' lay summary also argues for reducing that pressure.
edits.reason: Remove the story of the course guessing correctly. Distinguish the study's duration from the course's recovery estimate, while preserving the quotation.

files.review_note: Qualify the descriptive summary and reader-directed claims; keep moderators, practical examples and the setting limit.

edits.before: People don't ask because they think asking makes them look worse. It makes them look better, and the paper says the fear is misplaced in those words.
edits.after: In these experiments, people who asked for advice were judged more competent; task difficulty and whom they asked affected the result.
edits.reason: Scope the result to the experiments instead of promising that asking always improves an impression.

edits.before: Flynn and Lake, earlier in the same week, answer one of the two fears that keep an email in drafts — *they will say no*. This answers the other, which is usually the louder one: *they will think less of me for asking.* Both estimates run the same direction, and both are wrong the same way.
edits.after: Week 8 pairs this with Flynn and Lake for two worries that can keep an email in drafts: *will they say no?* and *will they think less of me for asking?* The studies examine different judgements; neither predicts the reply to a particular email.
edits.reason: Remove the unsupported ranking of fears and the claim that every reader's estimate is wrong.

edits.before: The three moderators are the useful part, because they are the week's only advice about **choosing who to write to** rather than how to format the message.
edits.after: The moderators help with **choosing who to write to**.
edits.reason: Remove the superlative and course bookkeeping; keep the practical connection.

edits.before: Note the setting: these are experiments on perceived competence in work and decision-making tasks, not a study of tutors, and the week says so rather than implying somebody measured a lecturer.
edits.after: These are experiments on perceived competence in work and decision-making tasks, not a study of university tutors.
edits.reason: Keep the research limit without praising the course for stating it.

files.review_note: Retain: concise study summary, association wording and a specific link to the switching line in the ledger.
Retain: three distinct model pathways and a clear link to partial disclosure; the list is substantive.
Keep the counterexample and narrow scope; cut the unsubstantiated claim about imbalance across the literature.

edits.before: It is not a general verdict on pragmatics and the week doesn't offer it as one. What it does do is put the question where week 2's double empathy problem already put it — a mismatch has two sides, and the side that assumes it sent a clear signal has not been tested nearly as often.

edits.reason: The preceding text makes the course connection. Cut a repeated thesis and an unsupported comparison of how often each side has been studied.

files.review_note: Retain: the three goals belong to the review and the course link is short.
Retain: the three effects are genuinely distinct, and the annotation already states dependence on disclosure and setting.
Shorten the course connection and preserve the abstract-only and population limits without claims about shared machinery.

edits.before: Week 10 cites it for the structural point and nothing more: disclosure is a set of levels rather than an on switch. That is the premise underneath the five audiences and underneath partial disclosure, and it is worth knowing that it isn't this course's invention — the shape was described decades ago, in a different literature, about different people.
edits.after: Week 10 uses the idea of levels of disclosure when distinguishing audiences and teaching partial disclosure.
edits.reason: The source is already identified; remove repeated assurances that the course did not invent the idea.

edits.before: Two limits, stated rather than glossed. Only the abstract was read, so the levels themselves are not reproduced here or in the lecture; the course names that they exist and teaches its own cut. And the population is people with psychiatric diagnoses, which is not the same population as autistic students, even though a great deal of the disclosure machinery turns out to be shared. Read across, not straight through.
edits.after: Only the abstract was read, so its levels are not reproduced here or in the lecture; the course teaches its own working model. The paper concerns psychiatric diagnoses. Its population and findings should not be treated as interchangeable with those of autism studies.
edits.reason: Keep both limits plainly. Remove self-congratulation about stating them and a broad claim about shared machinery.

Retain: the longer annotation earns its length by distinguishing staff perspectives, institutional responsibility and study limitations.
Retain: a useful complication of the course argument, stated plainly.

edits.before: Gender was non-significant (*r* = .01) and age negligible (*r* = .06), which disposes of two folk theories at once.
edits.after: Gender was non-significant (*r* = .01) and age negligible (*r* = .06).

edits.before: The finding week 5 leans on hardest is this: situational constructs accounted for greater variance in forgiveness than victims' dispositions. The week had been asserting that repair is error handling rather than a matter of character, and that the receiving side is a protocol rather than a personality. This is the evidence for it — what you do and say after an offence matters more than who the other person happens to be.
edits.after: Situational constructs accounted for greater variance in forgiveness than victims' dispositions. Week 5 uses this to focus on what happens during repair, rather than treating forgiveness as a fixed trait of the person receiving the apology.
edits.reason: State the finding and its teaching use without narrating how research vindicated an earlier course assertion.

Partners are assigned by the tutor to mix the room. Compare what each of you
recorded and what you inferred; keep any differences to revisit in week 11.
edits.reason: Preserve the mixed-classroom design and cross-week link without guaranteeing a difference or announcing the point.

edits.before:
A page of notes that passes the asleep test, and one written-down rule. Test
the rule this week, and Sunday's journal entry writes itself: what happened,
the rule, the test, the rule now.
edits.after:
A page of notes that passes the asleep test, and one written-down rule. Test
the rule this week, then use the result in Sunday's journal entry: what
happened, the rule, the test, the rule now.
edits.reason: Keep the deliverable and four-part format without promising that the writing will be effortless.

files.review_note: Keep the fictional-character rule, opt-out, run sheet and assessment work. Tighten two lines that explain intentions after the practical instruction is already clear.

edits.before:
Nobody discloses anything real in this lab. Every disclosure in the room
belongs to a character on a card. That's a rule, not a suggestion. It exists
so that practising the mechanics costs nothing you'd have to take back.
edits.after:
Nobody discloses anything real in this lab. Every disclosure belongs to a
character on a card, so you can practise without giving the room information
about yourself.
edits.reason: Keep the mandatory fiction boundary and its concrete purpose without escalating it through a second emphatic declaration.

edits.before:
Two draft sentences for a character, receiving practice, and a revised draft
protocol. If you do decide to say a need-without-label sentence of your own
this week, the Field Journal is where it goes: what you said, to whom, what came
back. That's your decision. The course only makes sure you have the sentence
ready.
edits.after:
Two draft sentences for a character, receiving practice, and a revised draft
protocol. If you choose to say a need-without-label sentence of your own this
week, you can use it for the Field Journal: what you said, to whom, what came
back.
edits.reason: The conditional already preserves choice; remove the repeated reassurance about what the course provides.

files.review_note: Keep short impact slides and deliberate teaching repetition. Align scope and reader-address changes with the lecture; simplify speaker notes that explain the course's virtue.

edits.before: - Pause here. Let the room notice that everyone already knows this, and nobody was told.
edits.after: - Pause here before showing a possible reply.
edits.reason: Preserve the pause without assuming every student already knows the convention.

edits.before: - Read it twice. It is the whole argument and it is on every page of the site.
edits.after: - Read it twice, pausing between the two clauses.
edits.reason: Keep the delivery instruction and remove the promotional explanation.

edits.before: - The run sheet promise matters to a lot of people in this room. Make it explicitly.
edits.after: - Say that the lab run sheets are available in advance.
edits.reason: Replace a prediction about the room with the information students need.

edits.before:
- This is the engineering scandal the course is named for.
- Researchers have been writing the rules down for over fifty years, for other researchers, in a register nobody outside the field reads.
edits.after: - Researchers have been writing the rules down for over fifty years, for other researchers.
edits.reason: The slide already carries the joke; the notes need only the supporting context.

edits.before: - We read the abstract, not the paper. Do not list the six; say so out loud, because the room should see the course obeying its own citation rule.
edits.after: - We read the abstract, not the paper. Say so; do not list the six.
edits.reason: Retain honest attribution without directing the teacher to perform the course's integrity.

edits.before: - The finding that survives is the one that matters here.
edits.reason: The slide states the finding; this note adds only emphasis.

edits.before:
The course's position is not "don't take it".

It is that you should be able to **see the fork while you're standing at it**.
edits.after:
**See the fork while you're standing at it.**

Then decide whether this is the conversation you want to start.
edits.reason: Keep the fork image and agency while removing institutional self-commentary.

edits.before: Everything so far assumes the opening **obliges** you. The course hasn't earned that yet.
edits.after: Why does an opening make a reply **expected**?
edits.reason: Align with the lecture's direct question.

edits.before: - This is the honest gap, and the room should watch you close it rather than paper over it.
edits.after: - Name the evidence gap before introducing Stivers and Rossano.
edits.reason: Turn a claim about honesty into a concrete teaching instruction.

edits.before: **If replies are hard for you:** you may have been treating every opening as maximum obligation. Many are turned down low. A nod answers a nod. You can match the level you were given.
edits.after: **If replies are hard for you:** you can match the level you were given. A nod can answer a nod; a person already walking away may not be inviting a conversation.
edits.reason: Carry through the lecture's removal of assumptions about the reader.

edits.before: - Collect the changes on the board: position, wording, timing, body. That list is the week's real artefact, and week 4 measures it in milliseconds.
edits.after: - Collect the changes on the board: position, wording, timing, body. Keep the list for week 4's work on timing.
edits.reason: Keep the board work and cross-reference; cut the repeated declaration of significance.

edits.before: If you run the handshake without effort, the spec read as the obvious. That's because you've run it ten thousand times, not because it's simple.
edits.after: If you run the handshake without effort, familiarity can make its rules hard to see.
edits.reason: Remove the invented count and align the slide with the lecture.

files.review_note: Keep slide structure, study results, field-note examples and the maintenance jokes. Align the notes with the lecture edits and stop scripting student agreement or mistakes.

edits.before: Week 1: we wrote the handshake down. Six lines, one branch nobody takes.
edits.after: Week 1: we wrote the handshake down. Six lines and a branch for a real answer.
edits.reason: Describe the existing branch without claiming nobody ever takes it.

edits.before: - The course's own observation: anyone whose implementation differs runs a small breach every day, unplanned.
edits.after: - The course's own observation: a mismatch can expose an expectancy without anyone setting out to test it.
edits.reason: Align the speaker note with the lecture's removal of a universal daily-experience claim.

edits.before: - Set this up as an experiment they can run at dinner. Ask a fluent user why they did something social. You will not get silence.
edits.after: - Suggest an experiment they can run at dinner: ask a fluent user why they did something social and record the answer.
edits.reason: Keep the experiment open instead of supplying its result in advance.

edits.before: - Which is why interviewing your way to the protocol does not work, and why this course observes instead.
edits.after: - Check the answer against observed exchanges. The next slide explains when reports can be accurate.
edits.reason: The original declares interviewing ineffective immediately before teaching an interview technique; make the transition support the stated evidence limit.

edits.before: - The left column invites them to theorise about people in general. They will, at length, and it will not be the rule.
edits.after: - The left column asks for a general explanation. Check either answer against actual exchanges.
edits.reason: Match the revised lecture and remove the guaranteed prediction about interviewees.

edits.before: - Being told about the bias did not repair the estimate. That is what makes it a finding rather than a saying.
edits.after: - Being told about the bias did not repair the estimate.
edits.reason: Keep the reported result and cut the explanation of why it is a finding.

edits.before:
- This is an argument about how the room is arranged, not a compliment to anyone in it.
- It is also why the labs are mixed on purpose. Week 11 is where that pays off.
edits.after:
- Ask who has learned this protocol recently and which steps they had to work out.
- The labs bring different experiences together; return to the comparison in week 11.
edits.reason: Replace self-commentary with a question that can test the proposed teaching connection.

edits.before: Famous. In every textbook. It would make the next rule sound inevitable.
edits.after: It would make the next rule sound inevitable.
edits.reason: Retain the setup for checking a convenient claim without the sweeping textbook assertion.

edits.before: - Set it up sincerely. Let them nod along, because they have all heard it.
edits.after: - Ask whether they have encountered this explanation before.
edits.reason: Do not script agreement or assume the whole class shares the same prior reading.

edits.before: - Nisbett is an author on the 1977 paper we just used and on the 1971 hypothesis we are now declining to use. That is what an argued literature looks like.
edits.after: - Nisbett is an author on both the 1977 paper we just used and the 1971 hypothesis we are now declining to use.
edits.reason: The bibliographic contrast carries the point without a closing declaration of what proper scholarship looks like.

edits.before: - This slide is the course applied to itself. Check the claim that would have been most convenient for you, first.
edits.after: - Check the claim that would have been most convenient for you, first.
edits.reason: Keep the useful research instruction and cut the praise of the course itself.

edits.before:
You write a field note when something **didn't go smoothly**.

The one condition where the effect appears is the condition your journal is written in.
edits.after: If an exchange **didn't go smoothly**, check your note for judgements of the other person's character.
edits.reason: Align with the revised lecture: journal entries need not concern failure, and negative valence is not established here as the only condition.

edits.before: - Sharper than the thing it replaced, and narrower. That trade is the whole method.
edits.after: - Keep the claim limited to the reported conditions; do not generalise it to every field note.
edits.reason: Replace an abstract statement of methodological virtue with a concrete limit for the teacher to maintain.

edits.before: - Say this plainly, because the slogan version gets repeated without it and a student will meet the slogan version this week.
edits.after: - Distinguish a mutual misunderstanding from a claim that neither person has any difficulty.
edits.reason: Retain the important distinction without forecasting what a student will encounter this week.

edits.before: - For the fluent half of the room: this is a result about what you do in the first few seconds, and it is the most actionable thing in the week for you.
edits.after: - Ask the fluent runners to examine their first impressions before treating them as evidence about the other person.
edits.reason: Do not attribute the study participants' behaviour to every fluent student or rank what they will find useful.

edits.before: - Point at "untested with". Naming the limit is what makes it a specification rather than an opinion, and it is the clause first entries leave out.
edits.after: - Point at "untested with". Ask students to name what remains untested in their own entries.
edits.reason: Keep the specific teaching cue and remove a repeated maxim plus a prediction of student omissions.

edits.before:
- Three are deliberately borderline. When the room splits, stop and let them argue. That is the useful part.
- Do not resolve all three. Leaving one open is honest and it gets written up in somebody's journal.
edits.after:
- Three are deliberately borderline. If the room splits, stop and compare the reasons.
- Do not resolve all three. Students can keep an unresolved case for their journal.
edits.reason: Preserve the discussion and unresolved case without prescribing the class's reaction or praising the exercise's honesty.

edits.before: - Nobody reads these out. Say that before they start writing, or they will write a safe one.
edits.after: - Nobody reads these out. Say that before they start writing.
edits.reason: Retain the privacy instruction without assuming how students would otherwise respond.

edits.before: - The left column is where their first entries will land. Say so now, so that seeing it in their own writing is recognition rather than failure.
edits.after: - Have students compare a sentence from their own entry with both columns.
edits.reason: Replace an invented forecast of student mistakes with an actual comparison.

edits.before: - Point at the third one. A course about undocumented rules marks which of its own rules are homemade.
edits.after: - Point at the third one: the asleep test is the course's rule of thumb, not a finding attributed to Milton or Sasson.
edits.reason: Preserve the useful attribution boundary without another statement of the course's consistency.

files.review_note: Align the deck and presenter notes with the edited lecture. Keep the entire spoken register break and its snap-back unchanged, alongside the tables, activities and study results.

edits.before: - The week the course is most careful, and the week with the most practical scripts. Both on purpose.
edits.after: - Introduce the five audiences and the choice to state a need without a label.
edits.reason: Replace self-praise in the opening delivery note with a concrete introduction.

edits.before: The mechanics work for all of them, because the evidence behind them does.
edits.after: Research on several concealable identities, alongside autism-specific studies.
edits.reason: Match the lecture’s source scope without promising that the scripts work for every situation.

edits.before:
- So observers in a lab say "tell people". The people deciding whether to tell say "it's complicated".
- Not contradictory. Different vantage points on the same transaction. This course won't pick one for them.
edits.after: - A favourable first impression does not settle whether disclosure will help at work. The studies ask different people about different consequences.
edits.reason: Do not turn study participants’ ratings into advice to disclose.

edits.before:
A list of reasons to be careful is not a decision aid. It is a thumb on one side of the scale.

So: what does **not** telling cost?
edits.after: What does **not** telling cost?
edits.reason: Let the ledger question lead into the study without another polished contrast.

edits.before: - Say this plainly. A week that only catalogues the risk of disclosing has decided for them while claiming not to.
edits.after: - Ask students to keep both telling and not telling in the ledger.
edits.reason: Give a teaching action rather than praise the lesson for avoiding bias.

edits.before: - Thirteen different identities, not one. This is a general finding about concealable things, which is why it belongs in a week that opened by saying the mechanics work for all of them.
edits.after: - The sample spans thirteen concealable identities. Keep that scope distinct from the autism-specific studies.
edits.reason: Retain the sample’s breadth without extrapolating to every concealable identity.

edits.before: - The obvious misreading is right there, so say the right one twice.
edits.after: - Name the predictor: anticipated stigma, not the effort of concealing.
edits.reason: Give the presenter the distinction directly without presuming a reader error.

edits.before:
- Tie it back to week 8: the support staff said the fix was structural. This is the measurement underneath their recommendation.
- It is also the one claim in this week that is not about what the student should do.
edits.after: - Connect this interpretation to week 8’s discussion of structural changes.
edits.reason: Remove an announcement of the lesson’s virtue and retain the useful cross-reference; the causal interpretation is flagged separately.

edits.before: - Say before they start that nothing gets read out. Otherwise they write a safe one.
edits.after: - Say before they start that nothing gets read out.
edits.reason: The privacy instruction stands without predicting what every student would otherwise write.

edits.before: - Slow down and mean it. This is the course putting the tool down, and a room can tell when it happens.
edits.after: - Slow down. Leave the examples time to register.
edits.reason: Preserve the deliberate delivery shift without claiming what the room will feel; none of the protected spoken text changes.

edits.before: - The week's most useful and least-taught idea. Say it once, plainly, then show it.
edits.after: - Say it once, then show the example.
edits.reason: Remove two unsupported superlatives while retaining the delivery instruction.

edits.before: - That first sentence gets the adjustment and changes exactly one piece of what they know. The rest stays theirs.
edits.after: - The first sentence asks for an adjustment without naming a diagnosis. The speaker chooses whether to share the rest.
edits.reason: Match the lecture’s distinction between requesting an adjustment and guaranteeing one.

edits.before: - The dashed slip is the whole idea: it is not in the envelope, and nothing in what you sent says one is missing.
edits.after: - Point to the dashed slip: the speaker has left the diagnosis out of the envelope.
edits.reason: Explain the drawing without promising control over the recipient’s inferences.

edits.before:
Costs almost nothing in week 1.

Costs a great deal to say for the first time in week 8.
edits.after: An option at the first group meeting or in the first week of a job: make the need part of the working arrangements before a problem needs explaining.
edits.reason: Remove the unmeasured universal cost claim while preserving the early-disclosure option.

edits.before: - Everyone in the room will be on this side of it at some point.
edits.reason: The receiving procedure does not need a prediction about everyone in the room.

edits.before: - Nobody reads either out. The show of hands is the whole result, and it is why the next section exists.
edits.after: - Nobody reads either sentence out. Collect only the show of hands.
edits.reason: Keep the activity boundary and cut commentary about the lesson’s structure.

edits.before:
- Reviewers writing down the prior their own field was running on, in the paper. That is the thing this entire course says nobody does.
- So the honest position for us is not "disclose" or "don't". It is: here are both columns, and it is your call.
edits.after: - Return to both ledger columns. The decision stays with the person disclosing.
edits.reason: The slide already states the review’s finding; the notes need not celebrate its resemblance to the course’s thesis.

edits.before: - This is the one audience where asking first costs nothing at all, which is why it is the one to practise on.
edits.after: - Rehearse the question before deciding what information to share.
edits.reason: Do not promise that contacting disability services is cost-free for everyone.

edits.before:
- Everybody in this room will be on the receiving side at some point, probably sooner than the other side.
- Watch for the re-reading coming up in their answers. If it does, that is the useful discovery, and it lands better from them than from me.
edits.after: - Listen for re-reading in the answers. If it appears, ask the pair to try the response again without it.
edits.reason: Replace predictions about students’ lives and reactions with an observable teaching action.

edits.before: Next week: interoperation, not conversion. The argument the whole course has been building to.
edits.after: Next week: interoperation, not conversion.
edits.reason: The transition works without another declaration of the course’s significance.
